title: Online civic space is narrowing through censorship, repression, shutdowns, and information manipulation across a majority of assessed countries
source_unit: Freedom House, Freedom on the Net 2025: An Uncertain Future for the Global Internet
geography: 72 countries assessed using country-level expert-coded internet-freedom indicators, covering the majority of the world's internet users

denominator.unit: countries assessed by Freedom on the Net 2025

consecutive_decline_years.unit: consecutive years of global internet-freedom decline reported by Freedom House

countries_deteriorated.unit: assessed countries where internet-freedom conditions deteriorated during the coverage period

countries_improved.unit: assessed countries where overall internet-freedom scores improved during the coverage period

free_status_group.unit: assessed countries classified as Free in internet freedom

observations.method: Freedom House country assessments using 21 indicators across obstacles to access, limits on content, and violations of user rights, with country researchers and advisors.
observations.uncertainty: The index is an expert-coded comparative assessment, not a direct measure of every user's experience, actual content exposure, or causal effect on political behavior; country coverage and scoring decisions shape comparability.
observations.subgroup: Internet users, journalists, activists, political opposition, minority groups, civil society, platform users, and populations in countries with different institutional and geopolitical conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Country scores can improve despite global decline, and legal protections, civil society, circumvention tools, independent media, or institutional checks can preserve meaningful online space in particular settings.

denominator.unit: countries covered by Freedom on the Net 2025 control indicators

political_arrests_or_imprisonment.unit: percent of the world's internet users living in countries where people were arrested or imprisoned for online political, social, or religious expression

online_activity_attacks_or_killings.unit: percent of internet users living in countries where people were attacked or killed for online activities

content_blocking.unit: percent of internet users living in countries where political, social, or religious content was blocked online

social_media_restriction.unit: percent of internet users living in countries where social-media access was temporarily or permanently restricted

network_disconnection.unit: percent of internet users living in countries where authorities disconnected internet or mobile networks, often for political reasons

observations.method: Country-level coding of repression, censorship, platform restriction, and network shutdown indicators, weighted in the report by country internet-user populations.
observations.uncertainty: These are population shares based on country classifications and internet-user estimates, not incidence rates for individuals; the indicators capture presence of a control environment rather than uniform exposure.
observations.subgroup: People expressing political, social, or religious views online; protesters; journalists; activists; minority communities; and internet users in countries employing shutdowns or content controls.
observations.counterinterpretation: A country-level control measure does not mean every user was censored or harmed; courts, private networks, encryption, circumvention, and local variation can create different practical experiences.

denominator.unit: countries assessed for online information manipulation and digital infrastructure controls

manipulation_mechanisms.value: paid commenters, imitation news sites, AI-generated misleading content, and undisclosed progovernment influencers

satellite_connectivity_risk.value: expanding satellite internet can connect rural and war-affected communities while exposing providers to government pressure over surveillance and censorship

key_control_domains.unit: key internet-control domains monitored by Freedom House

observations.method: Freedom House synthesis of country narratives and nine key internet-control domains, including information manipulation and emerging satellite connectivity.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies documented mechanisms and risks; it does not estimate the causal effect of each tactic on belief, turnout, protest, trust, or social cohesion.
observations.subgroup: Online audiences, independent media, activists, rural and war-affected communities, satellite providers, platforms, governments, and civil-society monitors.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital infrastructure can expand access, connection, and civic coordination even where manipulation and surveillance risks rise; control and empowerment can coexist in the same network.

related_sources.claim: Freedom House policy recommendations on rebuilding a free, open, and secure internet.
United States country assessment and score context.

boundary: This record adds an online-control-to-civic-space, information-manipulation, infrastructure, privacy, and political-capacity route. It is not respondent-level media-use data, does not establish individual persuasion or voting effects, and does not treat an expert-coded country score as direct proof of personal experience.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Freedom House 2025 report landing page, full report PDF, methodology/project page, policy recommendations, and selected country page were retrieved; global decline, country changes, control endpoints, information manipulation, and satellite-connectivity claims were cross-checked.
